When the heater stops doing its job

A Chicago condo can lose heat with the furnace still making noise. A house can feel cold even while air moves through the vents. The observations below help separate a repair request from an emergency and give the technician a useful starting point.

Furnace will not start Call today Diagnosis first

Likely causes

  • Thermostat is not calling for heat
  • Loss of electrical power to the furnace
  • Ignition fault or safety lockout

Check safely first

  • With no odor or alarm, check the thermostat is set to heat above room temperature.
  • Note whether the furnace is silent or tries to start.
  • Keep panels closed; avoid repeated resets or attempts to light the furnace.

What the technician does

The technician follows the start sequence to find where operation stops. A control or power problem differs from a failed part or safety shutdown. The technician identifies the failed stage and explains the proposed repair before a price is approved.

Diagnosis first

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Heater starts, then shuts off Call today Fault sets visit length

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow causing overheating
  • Flame detection or ignition fault
  • Control or thermostat signal problem

Check safely first

  • Note how soon heat stops and whether the fan keeps running.
  • Inspect an accessible filter only as the equipment instructions permit.
  • Do not bypass a safety switch or keep restarting the heater.

What the technician does

The technician checks whether the shutdown follows overheating, loss of flame, or a lost call for heat. Replacing a switch without identifying its trigger can leave the fault unresolved. The technician identifies the trigger and checks whether the shutdown returns during operation.

Fault sets visit length

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Heater runs but blows cold air Call today After diagnosis

Likely causes

  • Fan runs without a call for heat
  • Ignition fails while the fan operates
  • Safety shutdown interrupts heat production

Check safely first

  • Check whether the thermostat fan setting is continuous rather than automatic.
  • Note whether air stays cold through the heat call or only between cycles.
  • Keep the furnace closed and leave ignition checks to the technician.
  • If gas odor or a CO alarm appears, leave immediately.

What the technician does

Air movement does not prove that the furnace is producing heat. Brief fan operation between heat cycles differs from supply air that stays cold. The technician checks the heat demand and startup sequence to locate the interruption.

Scratching, grinding, or banging noise Call today Part-dependent

Likely causes

  • Worn motor or moving assembly
  • Loose or rubbing component
  • Abnormal ignition or operating sequence

Check safely first

  • Note whether the noise occurs at startup, during running, or at shutdown.
  • If safe, record the sound from outside the closed cabinet.
  • Stop using a heater with violent banging, smoke, or an electrical burning odor.

What the technician does

A noise heard through vents can originate at the furnace, so the loudest room is only a clue. The technician locates the sound and checks the associated moving parts. The technician identifies the noisy component and related damage before recommending repair or replacement.

Gas odor near the heater Emergency Emergency response first

Likely causes

  • Possible gas leak near the equipment
  • Possible leak elsewhere in the building
  • Unsafe ignition or combustion condition

Check safely first

  • Occupants should leave the building immediately.
  • From outside, call emergency services or the gas utility.
  • Avoid flames and electrical switches; do not try to locate or repair the leak.

What the technician does

Emergency responders or the gas utility must address the immediate danger first. Occupants should return only after clearance and should not restart the heater themselves. Heater repair then addresses any identified equipment fault or required corrective work. Scheduling a technician is not a substitute for the emergency response. City & Suburban offers emergency HVAC service until midnight except Sundays.

CO alarm sounds during heater use Emergency Emergency response first

Likely causes

  • Possible combustion or venting problem
  • Possible fault at another fuel-burning appliance
  • An alarm condition needing emergency assessment

Check safely first

  • Occupants should leave immediately, including anyone feeling unwell.
  • Call emergency services from outside the building.
  • Do not silence the alarm and continue using the heater.

What the technician does

A CO alarm cannot safely be diagnosed by smell or by whether the furnace still runs. Emergency responders assess the immediate danger before a repair visit proceeds. After clearance, the heater evaluation should address any equipment fault identified. A running fan, open window, or cleared fault display does not establish safe operation. Occupants should follow the responders' instructions about returning.

Safety switch trips or fault returns Call today Testing determines time

Likely causes

  • Overheating linked to restricted airflow
  • A venting or pressure-related fault
  • A control, wiring, or switch problem

Check safely first

  • Record the fault display if visible without opening the cabinet.
  • Note whether the fault follows startup or a longer run.
  • Do not jumper a switch, defeat a lockout, or repeatedly reset power.
  • If odor or an alarm occurs, leave rather than troubleshooting.

What the technician does

A safety switch may be stopping an unsafe operating condition. Replacing it without finding the trigger can leave that condition unresolved. The technician identifies the cause of the trip and checks the protection without bypassing the switch.

Heater runs with weak airflow Book soon Cause-dependent

Likely causes

  • Restricted filter or return-air path
  • Fan or motor operating problem
  • Air distribution fault outside the furnace

Check safely first

  • Check for furniture blocking accessible room vents.
  • Observe an accessible filter according to the equipment instructions.
  • Call promptly if weak airflow comes with shutdowns or falling indoor temperature.
  • Leave fan adjustments and internal cleaning to the technician.

What the technician does

A running heater with little air reaching occupied rooms may have a furnace fault or a distribution problem. The technician locates the restriction before recommending repair. Duct repair addresses a confirmed distribution defect.

Water appears near the furnace Call today Source must be found

Likely causes

  • Blocked condensate drainage on an applicable furnace
  • Leak from nearby plumbing or equipment
  • Drainage or connection fault needing diagnosis

Check safely first

  • Observe where water first appears without opening the furnace.
  • Note whether the leak occurs during a heat cycle.
  • Keep away from wet electrical equipment; do not touch wiring or switches nearby.
  • Avoid assuming the furnace caused water simply because the cabinet is wet.

What the technician does

Nearby pipes can leave water around a furnace without the furnace causing the leak. The technician traces the source and separates it from resulting damage. Report water reaching electrical components when requesting service.

Pricing

What determines heater repair cost?

Two furnaces blowing cold air can need different repairs. City & Suburban diagnoses the confirmed fault before quoting the exact price in writing for approval. The approved price has no hidden fees. Ask about the service-call charge and any credit toward an approved repair when booking.

1 The confirmed faultA heater that stops at ignition needs a different repair from one that overheats after running. Diagnosis determines which work belongs in the quote.
2 The replacement partThe equipment model and failed component determine the correct part. A motor assembly and a smaller control component involve different materials and labor.
3 Part availabilityA locally available part may allow repair during the visit. An ordered part can require a return appointment; availability should be explained before scheduling completion.
4 Access to the furnaceA clear basement cabinet and a tight hallway closet offer different working space. Safe access and room to reach the failed component affect the work.
5 Related faults or damageA single failed component differs from several connected faults. The technician identifies the necessary corrective work and explains any remaining concern before quoting.
6 Verification after repairInstalling a part is only part of the work. The repair needs operating checks that relate to the original fault, including whether the shutdown returns.

Keep fixing or consider replacement?

Repair the fault. Assess the whole furnace.

An isolated fault can justify repair when the rest of the furnace remains serviceable. Repeated shutdowns, major damage, or scarce parts can make replacement worth comparing. Age alone does not decide the outcome. Compare the diagnosed repair cost and existing heater condition with furnace replacement before choosing another repair.

The $5,000 rule compares furnace age multiplied by repair cost with a rough threshold. It is not a City & Suburban price or a safety test. A result above that threshold is a reason to compare furnace replacement, not an automatic instruction to replace.

What affects remaining furnace life?
Furnace age
Typical forced-air furnace service life: 15 to 20 years; condition still determines the decision.
Operating condition
A suspected cracked heat exchanger means the furnace stays off until a professional safety evaluation. A manufacturer-approved heat exchanger replacement can then be compared with full furnace replacement, where parts and warranty permit.
Repair history
Two or more no-heat failures in one season signal a need to compare repair with replacement.
Replacement parts
Discontinued or universal-only parts can become the practical limit on further repair.

Hallway closet furnace

An upflow furnace in a closet and a horizontal unit in an attic or crawlspace need different access for the same repair. Access affects labor time, not the diagnosis; keep the closet clear.

Existing home furnace

A high-efficiency condensing furnace has a condensate drain and plastic venting that a standard-efficiency furnace lacks, so the possible faults differ. The repair decision depends on the confirmed fault and overall condition.

Furnace with internal controls

A flame sensor, igniter, or control board fault can interrupt startup. The cabinet photo shows the furnace housing; internal testing belongs to a technician.

Thermostat

A heat call starts at the thermostat. Confirm settings before assuming a cold room means the furnace has failed.

Heater repair questions

How soon can City & Suburban reach a heater repair call in Chicago?

City & Suburban books same-day heater repair when the schedule allows, and runs emergency HVAC service every day till midnight, except Sundays. Calls go out across 21 service areas, 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs. Maintenance plan members get priority dispatch. Robert F. (Nov 2025) described the sequence: "My heater went out at 5am. I called after 7am, technician showed at 8:30 to verify the issue and what part was needed." A house with no heat in January is urgent work, not a routine booking.

Why do two furnace repairs on the same block cost different amounts?

The part decides most of it. An igniter or a flame sensor is a small, stocked item. A blower motor, an inducer assembly or a control board costs more and takes longer to fit. Access matters too: a furnace in a tight attic or a closet behind plumbing takes more time than one standing open in a basement. Age changes both the price and the supply of parts, and a system still inside its parts warranty changes the math again. City & Suburban diagnoses the fault first, then puts the exact price in writing for approval before any work starts. Current offers are listed in the pricing section.

What happens on a heater repair visit, from arrival to restart?

Diagnosis comes first. A NATE-certified technician works out which part failed on the furnace in the house, whatever the make or model. City & Suburban then puts the exact price in writing for approval, with no hidden fees added later. Where a repair is the right answer, the repair is what gets quoted rather than a replacement. Nothing is fitted before that price is approved. Ken D. (Apr 2026) described his visit: "Rob quickly diagnosed the problem, explained what was needed, went and grabbed the part and had my heat working in no time."

How long does a heater repair usually take?

Many repairs finish inside one visit, depending on the part, access and part availability. Swapping an igniter, a flame sensor, a pressure switch or a run capacitor is often under an hour, test cycle included. A blower motor, an inducer assembly or a control board can run two to three hours. It takes longer when the cabinet has to come apart. A part that is not at a local supply house turns the job into two visits. Simon W. (Apr 2024) saw that version: "Part was ordered for the furnace and he came out the very next day, issued fixed." City & Suburban prices the work upfront, with no hidden fees whether the fix takes one trip or two.

Which checks are safe to make at home before calling for furnace repair?

With a gas smell, smoke or a CO alarm, skip all checks: leave and call 911 or the gas utility from outside. Otherwise, a few checks are safe. Confirm the thermostat is set to heat and has working batteries. Find the furnace service switch, which looks like a light switch and is easy to flip by mistake. Look at the breaker if the panel is safely reachable; reset it once at most. Change an accessible filter only with power off as the manufacturer's instructions describe, since a clogged filter can trip the high limit. Gas valves, burners and flue pipes belong to a technician. Sneha R. (Mar 2022) recalled a call made "when we don't realize that the service switch is off". City & Suburban books same-day service when the schedule allows once those checks come up empty.

When is a heater fault a safety emergency rather than a repair call?

A gas smell, a burning smell that does not clear, soot around the cabinet, or a sounding carbon monoxide alarm is not a service booking. The step is to leave the building, then call the gas utility and 911 from outside. Illinois requires carbon monoxide alarms near the sleeping areas of a home, under the Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act. A working carbon monoxide alarm is a required last line of defense, not a test for a cracked heat exchanger. The crack is found by inspecting the heat exchanger and testing combustion during a heating cycle. City & Suburban sends NATE-certified technicians for that work, every day till midnight except Sundays.

Diagnosis comes before any price. A NATE-certified technician finds the cause, then City & Suburban puts the exact repair price in writing for approval, with no hidden fees added later. Ask about the service-call charge for that diagnosis visit when the appointment is booked. The price waits because one symptom has many causes. A furnace blowing cold air can be an ignition lockout, a dirty flame sensor, a tripped high limit, a failed inducer or a gas supply fault. A number quoted sight unseen has to guess at which. Lena H. (Jan 2026) put it plainly: "C&S Heating look for solutions to fix vs selling you unnecessary spare parts."

City & Suburban has been family-owned since 1952 and is run by Rob, the second generation of the founding family. Diagnosis comes before any quote, and the exact price goes in writing for approval before work starts, with no hidden fees. Technicians are NATE-certified, and the company repairs all makes and models. Some customers describe seeing the same technician on return visits; that is an individual experience, not a scheduling promise. Heather S. (Dec 2025) came back three times and wrote: "Same man, same excellent service."

Does City & Suburban repair heaters that another company installed?

Yes. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, and a system put in by another contractor is treated no differently. Repair parts are matched to the furnace in the house, not to a preferred label. A second opinion on a diagnosis is a reasonable request. Todd F. (May 2026) called for one and wrote: "Great experience. I called them for my second opinion. Fast, friendly and efficient service." A sealed-combustion condensing furnace, an older mid-efficiency unit and a horizontal attic furnace are all familiar ground.

Which Chicago homes does this heater repair service suit, and which need a different visit?

The service fits forced-air gas heat. That means furnaces in single-family houses, two-flats, condos and small multi-family buildings across 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs. A furnace with one failed part is the clearest fit. Homes heated by a boiler, and homes running a heat pump, are covered by separate services, because the parts and controls differ. A cracked heat exchanger is the other limit: the furnace should stay off until a safety evaluation, then a manufacturer-approved heat exchanger replacement is compared with a new furnace. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, so the label on the cabinet does not decide the fit.

What should a tenant or a landlord do when a rented unit loses heat?

Chicago sets a floor. The Heat Ordinance requires at least 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. between September 15 and June 1. Overnight the minimum is 66 degrees, under Municipal Code 13-196-410, where the landlord supplies the heat. The code also lists exceptions. Work in a rented unit needs the owner or the property manager to approve the price. City & Suburban puts that exact price in writing before any work starts, with no hidden fees added later. Sarah A. (Mar 2024) rented through one such winter: "He came, identified the problem, double-checked his work and was back with the part the same night."

What happens when a part for an older furnace is no longer made?

Parts for a twenty-year-old furnace can be discontinued, back-ordered, or sold only as a universal replacement that needs the controls rewired. At that point a repair stops being a simple part price, and the comparison with replacement is worth seeing on paper. One common rule of thumb multiplies system age by repair cost, and treats a result above $5,000 as a reason to compare replacement, not an automatic verdict. Mardi K. (Feb 2026) was given both numbers for a failing motor: "he said we could replace the motor or the whole furnace and gave us pricing for both". City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, including units that old.

Can a heater repair happen in the evening or over a weekend?

Yes, within limits. City & Suburban runs emergency HVAC service every day till midnight, except Sundays. A Friday evening failure or a Saturday no-heat call is normal work, not an exception. Sunday is the gap. russell k. (Mar 2026) saw that: "I called on a Sunday night because my furnace wasn't working. The repair person was here first thing on Monday morning." Heather S. (Dec 2025) lost heat on a Saturday and wrote, "He was here at 9am that day to fix it."

Is a City & Suburban heater repair guaranteed if the fault comes back?

A fault that returns after a repair should go back to the company that made it, with the original invoice. Before approving a City & Suburban repair, ask what parts and labor coverage applies to the repaired component and for how long; that term belongs in writing alongside the price. Replacement parts may also carry manufacturer coverage, which is separate from the system's own warranty. Noah W. (Jul 2026) wrote after two visits more than five years apart: "They addressed our needs, answered our questions, and didn't try to upsell us."

What prevents the same no-heat call next winter?

Many no-heat calls start with something a pre-season check could have caught. A restricted filter chokes airflow and trips the high limit, which shows up as short cycling. A fouled flame sensor drops the burners seconds after ignition. Igniters and capacitors wear with use, but age alone does not predict when one fails; testing shows their condition. A furnace tune-up before the first cold night tests those parts under load and replaces the filter. A maintenance plan puts that visit on a seasonal schedule and adds priority dispatch. City & Suburban runs both. Maintenance can reduce avoidable failures, but it cannot prevent every one.

What proof is there that these furnace repairs hold up?

The record is public. City & Suburban averages 4.98 across 204 Google reviews and holds 4.9 from 251 reviews on Yelp. The company carries a BBB A+ rating. Repeat visits are the stronger signal. Noah W. (Jul 2026) wrote: "City & Suburban has serviced our HVAC system twice, over 5 years apart. Each experience was positive. They addressed our needs, answered our questions, and didn't try to upsell us." A furnace Sarah A. (Mar 2024) had fixed in a single day then "worked for years".

When the heater stops doing its job

A Chicago condo can lose heat with the furnace still making noise. A house can feel cold even while air moves through the vents. The observations below help separate a repair request from an emergency and give the technician a useful starting point.

Furnace will not start Call today Diagnosis first

Likely causes

  • Thermostat is not calling for heat
  • Loss of electrical power to the furnace
  • Ignition fault or safety lockout

Check safely first

  • With no odor or alarm, check the thermostat is set to heat above room temperature.
  • Note whether the furnace is silent or tries to start.
  • Keep panels closed; avoid repeated resets or attempts to light the furnace.

What the technician does

The technician follows the start sequence to find where operation stops. A control or power problem differs from a failed part or safety shutdown. The technician identifies the failed stage and explains the proposed repair before a price is approved.

Diagnosis first

Heater starts, then shuts off Call today Fault sets visit length

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow causing overheating
  • Flame detection or ignition fault
  • Control or thermostat signal problem

Check safely first

  • Note how soon heat stops and whether the fan keeps running.
  • Inspect an accessible filter only as the equipment instructions permit.
  • Do not bypass a safety switch or keep restarting the heater.

What the technician does

The technician checks whether the shutdown follows overheating, loss of flame, or a lost call for heat. Replacing a switch without identifying its trigger can leave the fault unresolved. The technician identifies the trigger and checks whether the shutdown returns during operation.

Fault sets visit length

Heater runs but blows cold air Call today After diagnosis

Likely causes

  • Fan runs without a call for heat
  • Ignition fails while the fan operates
  • Safety shutdown interrupts heat production

Check safely first

  • Check whether the thermostat fan setting is continuous rather than automatic.
  • Note whether air stays cold through the heat call or only between cycles.
  • Keep the furnace closed and leave ignition checks to the technician.
  • If gas odor or a CO alarm appears, leave immediately.

What the technician does

Air movement does not prove that the furnace is producing heat. Brief fan operation between heat cycles differs from supply air that stays cold. The technician checks the heat demand and startup sequence to locate the interruption.

Scratching, grinding, or banging noise Call today Part-dependent

Likely causes

  • Worn motor or moving assembly
  • Loose or rubbing component
  • Abnormal ignition or operating sequence

Check safely first

  • Note whether the noise occurs at startup, during running, or at shutdown.
  • If safe, record the sound from outside the closed cabinet.
  • Stop using a heater with violent banging, smoke, or an electrical burning odor.

What the technician does

A noise heard through vents can originate at the furnace, so the loudest room is only a clue. The technician locates the sound and checks the associated moving parts. The technician identifies the noisy component and related damage before recommending repair or replacement.

Likely causes

  • Possible gas leak near the equipment
  • Possible leak elsewhere in the building
  • Unsafe ignition or combustion condition

Check safely first

  • Occupants should leave the building immediately.
  • From outside, call emergency services or the gas utility.
  • Avoid flames and electrical switches; do not try to locate or repair the leak.

What the technician does

Emergency responders or the gas utility must address the immediate danger first. Occupants should return only after clearance and should not restart the heater themselves. Heater repair then addresses any identified equipment fault or required corrective work. Scheduling a technician is not a substitute for the emergency response. CO alarm sounds during heater use Emergency Emergency response first

Likely causes

  • Possible combustion or venting problem
  • Possible fault at another fuel-burning appliance
  • An alarm condition needing emergency assessment

Check safely first

  • Occupants should leave immediately, including anyone feeling unwell.
  • Call emergency services from outside the building.
  • Do not silence the alarm and continue using the heater.

What the technician does

A CO alarm cannot safely be diagnosed by smell or by whether the furnace still runs. Emergency responders assess the immediate danger before a repair visit proceeds. After clearance, the heater evaluation should address any equipment fault identified. A running fan, open window, or cleared fault display does not establish safe operation. Occupants should follow the responders' instructions about returning.

Safety switch trips or fault returns Call today Testing determines time

Likely causes

  • Overheating linked to restricted airflow
  • A venting or pressure-related fault
  • A control, wiring, or switch problem

Check safely first

  • Record the fault display if visible without opening the cabinet.
  • Note whether the fault follows startup or a longer run.
  • Do not jumper a switch, defeat a lockout, or repeatedly reset power.
  • If odor or an alarm occurs, leave rather than troubleshooting.

What the technician does

A safety switch may be stopping an unsafe operating condition. Replacing it without finding the trigger can leave that condition unresolved. The technician identifies the cause of the trip and checks the protection without bypassing the switch.

  • Fan or motor operating problem

Check safely first

  • Call promptly if weak airflow comes with shutdowns or falling indoor temperature.

A running heater with little air reaching occupied rooms may have a furnace fault or a distribution problem. The technician locates the restriction before recommending repair. Duct repair addresses a confirmed distribution defect.

  • Keep away from wet electrical equipment; do not touch wiring or switches nearby.
  • Avoid assuming the furnace caused water simply because the cabinet is wet.

What the technician does

Nearby pipes can leave water around a furnace without the furnace causing the leak. The technician traces the source and separates it from resulting damage. Report water reaching electrical components when requesting service.

Heater repair questions

How soon can City & Suburban reach a heater repair call in Chicago?

City & Suburban books same-day heater repair when the schedule allows, and runs emergency HVAC service every day till midnight, except Sundays. Calls go out across 21 service areas, 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs. Maintenance plan members get priority dispatch. Robert F. (Nov 2025) described the sequence: "My heater went out at 5am. I called after 7am, technician showed at 8:30 to verify the issue and what part was needed." A house with no heat in January is urgent work, not a routine booking.

Why do two furnace repairs on the same block cost different amounts?

The part decides most of it. An igniter or a flame sensor is a small, stocked item. A blower motor, an inducer assembly or a control board costs more and takes longer to fit. Access matters too: a furnace in a tight attic or a closet behind plumbing takes more time than one standing open in a basement. Age changes both the price and the supply of parts, and a system still inside its parts warranty changes the math again. City & Suburban diagnoses the fault first, then puts the exact price in writing for approval before any work starts. Current offers are listed in the pricing section.

What happens on a heater repair visit, from arrival to restart?

Diagnosis comes first. A NATE-certified technician works out which part failed on the furnace in the house, whatever the make or model. City & Suburban then puts the exact price in writing for approval, with no hidden fees added later. Where a repair is the right answer, the repair is what gets quoted rather than a replacement. Nothing is fitted before that price is approved. Ken D. (Apr 2026) described his visit: "Rob quickly diagnosed the problem, explained what was needed, went and grabbed the part and had my heat working in no time."

How long does a heater repair usually take?

Many repairs finish inside one visit, depending on the part, access and part availability. Swapping an igniter, a flame sensor, a pressure switch or a run capacitor is often under an hour, test cycle included. A blower motor, an inducer assembly or a control board can run two to three hours. It takes longer when the cabinet has to come apart. A part that is not at a local supply house turns the job into two visits. Simon W. (Apr 2024) saw that version: "Part was ordered for the furnace and he came out the very next day, issued fixed." City & Suburban prices the work upfront, with no hidden fees whether the fix takes one trip or two.

Which checks are safe to make at home before calling for furnace repair?

With a gas smell, smoke or a CO alarm, skip all checks: leave and call 911 or the gas utility from outside. Otherwise, a few checks are safe. Confirm the thermostat is set to heat and has working batteries. Find the furnace service switch, which looks like a light switch and is easy to flip by mistake. Look at the breaker if the panel is safely reachable; reset it once at most. Change an accessible filter only with power off as the manufacturer's instructions describe, since a clogged filter can trip the high limit. Gas valves, burners and flue pipes belong to a technician. Sneha R. (Mar 2022) recalled a call made "when we don't realize that the service switch is off". City & Suburban books same-day service when the schedule allows once those checks come up empty.

When is a heater fault a safety emergency rather than a repair call?

A gas smell, a burning smell that does not clear, soot around the cabinet, or a sounding carbon monoxide alarm is not a service booking. The step is to leave the building, then call the gas utility and 911 from outside. Illinois requires carbon monoxide alarms near the sleeping areas of a home, under the Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act. A working carbon monoxide alarm is a required last line of defense, not a test for a cracked heat exchanger. The crack is found by inspecting the heat exchanger and testing combustion during a heating cycle. City & Suburban sends NATE-certified technicians for that work, every day till midnight except Sundays.

Diagnosis comes before any price. A NATE-certified technician finds the cause, then City & Suburban puts the exact repair price in writing for approval, with no hidden fees added later. (Jan 2026) put it plainly: "C&S Heating look for solutions to fix vs selling you unnecessary spare parts."

City & Suburban has been family-owned since 1952 and is run by Rob, the second generation of the founding family. A second opinion on a diagnosis is a reasonable request. Todd F. (May 2026) called for one and wrote: "Great experience. I called them for my second opinion. Fast, friendly and efficient service." A sealed-combustion condensing furnace, an older mid-efficiency unit and a horizontal attic furnace are all familiar ground.

Chicago sets a floor. The Heat Ordinance requires at least 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. between September 15 and June 1. Overnight the minimum is 66 degrees, under Municipal Code 13-196-410, where the landlord supplies the heat. The code also lists exceptions. Parts for a twenty-year-old furnace can be discontinued, back-ordered, or sold only as a universal replacement that needs the controls rewired. At that point a repair stops being a simple part price, and the comparison with replacement is worth seeing on paper. Many no-heat calls start with something a pre-season check could have caught. A restricted filter chokes airflow and trips the high limit, which shows up as short cycling. A fouled flame sensor drops the burners seconds after ignition. Igniters and capacitors wear with use, but age alone does not predict when one fails; testing shows their condition. A furnace tune-up before the first cold night tests those parts under load and replaces the filter. A maintenance plan puts that visit on a seasonal schedule and adds priority dispatch. City & Suburban runs both. Maintenance can reduce avoidable failures, but it cannot prevent every one.
